extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, scholars, and law students interested in comparative doctrine of equivalents
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative analysis of legal standards for determining patent infringement under the doctrine of equivalents (UK, Germany, and U.S.), including tests, factual inquiries, and limiting doctrines such as prior art and prosecution estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improver three-question framework (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: The English Patents Court framed equivalency analysis as a three-question inquiry; the first two are factual background and the third is an exception that can limit claim interpretation to the literal meaning of the claim's words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Hoffmann viewed the third question as 'a question to be asked in all cases of infringement by equivalence' and emphasized that the first two questions merely provide background against which the third should be asked. The third question can, in certain circumstances, force the court to limit the scope of the claim to the strict literal meaning of the claim's words (and thus defeat a claim of equivalence). In Epilady, the third question led to a literalist result despite factual answers to the first two favoring equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: German two-question test (Epilady)
rubrics_metrics.description: The German court asked (1) whether the accused device has the identical effect of the claimed means (i.e., is it an equivalent), and (2) whether that equivalent would have been an obvious equivalent to a person skilled in the art when the patent was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court used the patent claim to determine the patent's 'teaching' and required that each essential feature in the claim be embodied by the accused device either literally or by equivalence. The second question requires assessing, prospectively at the time of grant, whether a skilled person, using professional knowledge and orienting to the meaning of the claims, would be able to detect the modified means as an identical-in-effect solution to the underlying problem. The German approach was described as aligning with Article 69(1) EPC and the Protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven-feature claim-teaching analysis (Epilady claim 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining the patent's 'teaching' the court identified seven essential features from claim 1 that must be embodied (literally or by equivalence): (1) hand-held portable housing; (2) motor means in housing; (3) helical spring comprising plurality of adjacent windings; (4) windings arranged to be driven in rotational sliding motion relative to skin; (5) spring includes an arcuate hair-engaging portion (a. arcuate, b. convex side where windings are spread apart, c. concave side where windings are pressed together); (6) rotational motion produces continuous motion of windings from spread apart to pressed together for engagement and plucking of hair; (7) surface velocity of windings relative to skin greatly exceeds surface velocity of housing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish infringement the accused product must embody each of these features exactly or in equivalent form. The German court found features 1 and 2 literal and 3–7 satisfied by equivalents (rubber rod considered a replacement means equivalent to coil spring). This shows a feature-by-feature assessment requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every claim limitation must be present or a substantial equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement, every limitation set forth in a claim must be found in the accused product or process exactly or by a substantial equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority (e.g., Johnston v. IVAC) and applied in both German and U.S. contexts; reinforces element-by-element analysis rather than holistic comparison of the invention as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. function-way-result (three-prong) test
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law, the doctrine of equivalents permits finding infringement if the accused device performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain substantially the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three prongs (function, way, result) must be met for equivalence of a claim element. The doctrine focuses on each claim element individually; therefore the patentee must show the presence of every essential element or its substantial equivalent. Example analysis: helical spring vs. rubber rod — function and result met clearly; 'way' requires mechanistic comparison (arcuate deformation causing openings, rotation producing gripping and plucking). A federal court would likely find the 'way' substantially the same in that example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine focuses on claim elements, not invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalency analysis is performed element-by-element; the doctrine does not focus on the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of infringement requires the patentee to show the presence of every essential element or its substantial equivalent in the accused device; thus courts analyze each limitation separately under equivalents tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art standard and temporal perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalency and obviousness-of-equivalence inquiries are judged from the viewpoint of a person skilled in the art using the professional knowledge available at the time the patent was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: German court emphasized that the skilled person, orientating to the meaning of the patent claims and using professional knowledge, must be able to detect the modified means as delivering an identical-in-effect solution. This temporal lens (at grant) matters for the 'obvious equivalent' inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical-in-effect requirement (German formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The German court required that the accused means be 'identical in effect' to the claimed means to be considered an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court stated it 'had no doubt the rubber rod was an equivalent based on the fact that the rubber rod "is identical in effect to a device making use of the wording of claim 1 of the patent in suit."' This places emphasis on functional/operational identity as a threshold for equivalence under German approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art limitation on equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents if the asserted scope of equivalency would encompass the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must examine cited prior patents and prior-art devices; if granting equivalence would cover what was already known, equivalence cannot be allowed. The article analyzes the prior art cited in the Improver patent as an illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel (file-wrapper estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage surrendered during prosecution with the patent office cannot be recaptured through equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history estoppel prevents a patentee from broadening claim scope via equivalents to reclaim subject matter given up during examination. Determining what was given up may require reviewing the prosecution history (not undertaken in the article for Improver).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and equivalents-clause can limit claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent's specification and any 'equivalents' clause may nonetheless constrain claim scope if a skilled reader would interpret the patentee as confining the claim to the literal meaning of a term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dr. Laming's testimony that the Improver specification referred only to 'helical spring' and lacked language suggesting alternatives; Justice Hoffmann accepted that a skilled reader would interpret 'helical spring' literally despite an equivalents clause referencing 'other specific forms' and asking readers to look to appended claims. Thus specification detail and how alternatives are (not) signaled can defeat a broad generic construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic 'way' analysis — use of examples to determine 'way' prong
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the 'way' prong involves detailed mechanistic description of how the claimed element operates (e.g., how arcuate form and rotational motion produce gaps, grip hairs, and pluck them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article models this analysis by describing how both the helical spring and the rubber rod deform when held arcuately, how gaps open/close on convex/concave sides, and how rotation causes hairs to enter gaps and be plucked; this type of technical comparison supports a finding that the 'way' is substantially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC/Protocol alignment as interpretive constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may frame equivalence analyses to align with Article 69(1) of the EPC and the Protocol on interpretation, influencing national approaches to claim scope and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The German court explicitly stated its inquiry was intended to align German patent law with Article 69(1) EPC and the Protocol. Different understandings of the Protocol by national courts (UK vs Germany) produce divergent scopes of protection and pose harmonization challenges; WIPO's draft Patent Harmonization Treaty (Article 21) seeks to define equivalence consistent with EPC Protocol concepts.
